title: v0: a maintenance-free time-series table on S3
description: Open Iceberg tables on any object store with compaction, dedup, retention and a last-value index built in, read faster than naive S3 Tables or Lance.
summary: The first version: open Iceberg tables on any object store with time-series layout and maintenance built in, and a reader with a last-value index, faster than naive S3 Tables or Lance for time series. Implemented 2026-10-12 with its exit criteria met, and released as 0.1.0.

title: Fast first queries on object storage
description: First queries on S3 in one or two round trips instead of six or seven, repeat queries from a local cache, and scans that read and decode less.
summary: The ordered steps P1–P8 that took first queries on S3 from six or seven dependent round trips to one or two, and repeat queries to local speed. Each step landed only if it improved first-run latency or requests without slowing other queries, and plain DuckDB still reads every table. The history of each step and its effect is on the docs page "Performance history"; measurements are in [`bench/results/PERFORMANCE.md`](../../bench/results/PERFORMANCE.md).

title: Installable, upgradable, switchable
description: Install from crates.io, PyPI and npm, upgrade tables without data loss, and turn every feature on or off with a setting.
summary: Timelake became something to install and keep running: every release on the usual registries, tables that record their format version and upgrade without data loss, and one registry of settings that turns each feature on or off per table, session or call. Releases follow [releases](../releases.md).

title: Exact answers before compaction
description: Rows sent twice count once, from the moment they land: dedup on read, an insertion time per row, and cold partitions compacted sooner.
summary: Devices resend data, and compaction runs later. The Timelake reader keeps only the latest write of each reading from the moment it lands, each row records when it arrived, compaction never lets an older write win, and partitions that are no longer written are compacted sooner so dedup on read only touches recent data.

title: Writes from JavaScript
description: Append to tables and keep them compacted from Cloudflare Workers and other JavaScript runtimes, in fixed memory.
summary: Append to and maintain tables from Cloudflare Workers, Node, Deno, Bun and browsers with the WebAssembly library. The write path and the streaming compaction it needed (memory of one batch per input, so a 128 MB Worker can compact a day) are shared with the engine, which got 4× less memory and 3× faster compaction from it.

title: Time-series SQL
description: Rollups that answer queries exactly, time-weighted averages, counters, downsampling, gap filling, and the rest of the function library.
summary: The queries time-series users write every day, exact and fast: rollups kept up to date and used automatically, time-weighted means and integrals of irregular readings, counters across resets, time in a state, downsampling with `m4`, gap filling, and gaps in the readings. Built so far: everything but the planned functions of the library (quantiles, ASOF and the rest, [spec 28](../0028-function-library.md)) and percentiles in rollups.

title: Millions of series
description: Ingest, latest values and dashboards that stay flat from thousands to millions of series, measured at each size.
summary: Requirement R27 ([purpose and requirements](../purpose.md)): a typical deployment has about 20,000 devices with 5–20 metrics each (100k–400k series); the top end is millions of devices with hundreds of metrics each (hundreds of millions of series). Everything that grows with the number of series must hold up at both: the last-value index, rollups, join filters, planning. Was P10 of the performance plan.

title: Benchmarks against every alternative
description: Every run kept with its commit, a weekly run on a fixed machine, and an industrial IoT benchmark against InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, ClickHouse and QuestDB with the monthly cost of each.
summary: Benchmarks anyone can rerun, against every alternative, that publish where Timelake loses as well as where it wins and report cost and growth next to latency (D21): the timebench harness with TSBS IoT and DevOps, every run on the website with its commit, a weekly run on one fixed machine, and an industrial IoT workload with checked answers. Still open: the public benchmarks not yet run, expert-written Iceberg, a run per object store, and side-by-side demos on the website.

title: Tuned on real data
description: A beta on a production industrial dataset with parallel writers fed from Kinesis: throughput, latency, and cost measured, then tuned for.
summary: Run Timelake on a production-like industrial dataset with parallel writers fed from a Kinesis stream, measure ingest, commit contention, latency and cost on real access patterns, and tune the defaults from what it shows. Was P9 of the performance plan, after the scan tuning and the remaining rollup work.

title: Any engine can attach
description: An Iceberg REST catalog, so Snowflake, Trino, Athena, and Spark query tables in place, and a DuckDB extension with Timelake's speedups and functions.
summary: Plain engines already read Timelake tables from the bucket. This milestone lets them attach the way they expect: an Iceberg REST catalog that Snowflake, Trino, Athena and Spark connect to, a DuckDB extension with dedup on read and the function library, Snowflake set up in one command, and documented patterns for many tenants.

title: Data lifecycle
description: Bring history in from TimescaleDB, Iceberg, or S3 Tables and publish it at once, adopt existing tables, and delete or erase data with an audit trail.
summary: Everything a table's data goes through besides appends: importing history from files and databases with a cutover, backfilling it into a live table in one atomic publish, adopting existing Iceberg tables, deletes that are audited and can be undone, GDPR erasure within 7 days, and the other times a reading carries.

title: Seconds-fresh data and ingestion
description: New rows visible within a second, before they are committed; MQTT, HTTP, and Kafka in, with rules and alerts as data arrives.
summary: Data visible to readers within a second of being written, through an object-store WAL or a managed hot store, and an ingestion pipeline that takes MQTT, HTTP and Kafka, evaluates rules as data arrives, and turns data into events on any stream.

title: Technical preview
description: Timelake open for anyone to try on real workloads, labelled a technical preview, once tuning on real data, the engine connections, the data lifecycle and seconds-fresh ingestion are in.
summary: A technical preview open to anyone: Timelake installed from the usual registries and run on real workloads, labelled a preview, with its limits and what may still change written down. It opens once most of what a team needs is in: the milestones before it on the roadmap (tuned on real data, any engine can attach, data lifecycle, seconds-fresh data and ingestion). Its specs are theirs, so its progress is theirs.

title: AI agents
description: AI agents query your data within the permissions you set, and a benchmark of whether they answer better, and for less, when it's in Timelake.
summary: An MCP server and client operations that let LLM agents find, understand and read time-series data within permission sets, and a benchmark that measures whether agents answer questions about the data more correctly, with fewer tokens, when it's in Timelake.

title: Apps and dashboards
description: Small ready-made files for frontends, refreshed on every write, and your Python functions applied automatically like rollups.
summary: Dashboards' usual requests answered by one GET from read models regenerated on each commit, and computed metrics: user-defined Python functions whose results Timelake keeps up to date the way it keeps rollups.

title: Edge and devices
description: Write on devices and gateways; Timelake moves the data to the lake and serves recent data when the uplink is down.
summary: Devices write to a local table and a sync agent moves committed data to the lake, store and forward; a gateway on site takes data, metrics, logs and blobs, runs rules locally, and serves recent data from its cache when the uplink is down.

title: Server mode
description: Timelake as a database on one machine, with the bucket as the copy. Then TSBS run with its own tools, next to published results.
summary: An experiment first: the same engine as one long-lived server on local NVMe, with the bucket as the durable copy and Postgres wire and Flight SQL protocols, measured against TimescaleDB before anything is built. It also lets TSBS run with its own loader and query runner, for numbers next to published results.

title: Any table format, any file format
description: The engine reaches tables and data files through lakekit's boundaries, Iceberg and Parquet by default, Vortex once Iceberg lists it.
summary: The engine stops assuming Iceberg and Parquet: tables go through lakekit's common table view, and data files through its `FileFormat` trait, shared with lakeglass. Iceberg and Parquet stay the defaults, so every engine that reads Timelake tables today still does. Vortex data files come once Iceberg's spec lists the format.
